FINANCIAL AI / OPEN QUESTION

When financial AI starts acting, who owns the decision?

Nandini Thakur · 3 min read

An agent that can act on a financial decision is an interesting idea. “It seemed confident” is a less interesting explanation afterwards.

One question running through my fintech exploration is how systems might move from prediction to recommendation and, in some settings, execution. I’m treating that as a direction to investigate, not a claim that every financial decision should be automated.

What exactly is being delegated?

Summarising a document, flagging a change, proposing an action, and taking that action are different responsibilities. Before thinking about an agent’s architecture, I want to understand its permission boundary. What can it see? What can it change? When does it have to stop and ask a person?

The less glamorous questions

I’m interested in the data trail behind a conclusion, the limits on an action, and the person who remains accountable. How would I investigate a bad outcome? How would the system behave when the situation no longer resembles the examples it was built around?

These questions make the project harder. That is probably a useful sign. A polished demo can skip the awkward conversation; a real financial workflow eventually has it.

A place to begin

A research assistant that connects a claim to its sources feels like a useful starting experiment. I’d want to observe where it helps, where it confidently fills a gap, and what a human needs to verify. I’m more interested in learning that boundary than in giving the system a bigger job title.

The technical work and the financial judgment belong together. That is the part I want to understand deeply.

Still thinking this through. A good counterargument is welcome.
